---
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:nil}
Let $S\ne\{0\}$ be a finite nilpotent semigroup.  Then $\mathcal P(S)$ is finitely
based if and only if $\mathbf N(S)$ has finite duality.  If finite duality fails,
then for every $k\ge1$ there is a finite ai-semiring satisfying all
identities of $\mathcal P(S)$ involving at most $k$ variables but failing another
identity of $\mathcal P(S)$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:comm}
If $S\ne\{0\}$ is finite and commutative with nilpotency index $d$, then
\[
 \mathcal P(S)\ \text{is finitely based}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists a\in S\ \ (a^{d-1}\ne0).
\]
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:product}
For every finite commutative nilpotent semigroup $N$,
\[
 \mathcal P(N\times C_2)\ \text{is finitely based}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \mathcal P(N)\ \text{is finitely based}.
\]
For arbitrary finite nilpotent $N$, finite basis of $\mathcal P(N\times C_2)$
implies finite basis of $\mathcal P(N)$.  If $N\ne\{0\}$ has nilpotency index $d$
and $a^{d-1}\ne0$ for some $a\in N$, then $\mathcal P(N\times C_2)$ is finitely
based without a commutativity assumption.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:empty}
Suppose $\mathcal P(S)\models w\preceq Q$, and put $W=c(w)$.  Delete from $Q$ all
words using variables outside $W$, and call the resulting set $Q_W$.  Then
$Q_W\ne\varnothing$ and
\[
 \mathcal P(S)\models w\preceq Q_W.
\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Assign the variables outside $W$ the empty set.  This proves validity after
the deletion.  If no word remained, assign every variable in $W$ an arbitrary
nonempty singleton.  The left side is then nonempty while the right side is
empty, a contradiction.  The empty right side in this argument is only a
value of a term, not a constant in the language.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:closure}
Write $c=c_k$.  Then
\begin{gather}
 uc(X)v\subseteq c(uXv),\qquad c(X)c(Y)\subseteq c(XY),\label{eq:nucleus}\\
 c(c(X)\cup c(Y))=c(X\cup Y),\qquad
 c(c(X)c(Y))=c(XY).\label{eq:quotient}
\end{gather}
The closed subsets of $U$ form a finite ai-semiring $B_k$ with operations
\[
 C\oplus D=c(C\cup D),\qquad C\otimes D=c(CD),
\]
and $X\mapsto c(X)$ is a surjective semiring homomorphism.  This quotient
satisfies every identity of $A$ involving at most $k$ variables.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
If a closure derivation is given, adding fixed left and right contexts to
each step gives another instance of \eqref{eq:closure-rule}.  Induction on
the length of the derivation yields the first inclusion in
\eqref{eq:nucleus}.  Hence $c(X)Y\subseteq c(XY)$.  For $x\in c(X)$,
\[
 x c(Y)\subseteq c(xY)\subseteq c(c(X)Y)\subseteq c(XY),
\]
which gives the second inclusion.  The equalities in \eqref{eq:quotient}
follow from monotonicity, extensivity, and idempotence together with
\eqref{eq:nucleus}.  The quotient operations are therefore well defined,
and all ai-semiring identities pass through the surjective homomorphism.

For a valid absorption identity $w\preceq Q$ and closed-set values $C_i$,
the set $c(Q(C_i))$ contains the original premise $Q(C_i)$.  The rule with
empty contexts therefore puts $w(C_i)$ inside this closure; taking closure
once more gives the absorption identity in the quotient.  Decomposing an
identity into absorption identities proves the last assertion.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:map}
If $h:U\to S$ is a semigroup homomorphism and $T\subseteq S$, then
$h^{-1}(T)$ is closed under all the rules above.  Indeed, $h$ induces a
homomorphism of full power semirings, and both the target absorption identity
and its left and right multiplicative contexts are valid.  No subsemigroup
assumption on $T$ is needed.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:normal}
The identities $L_d$ imply:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item any two long words with the same support are equal;
\item if $u$ and $v$ are long and $c(v)\subseteq c(u)$, then $u\preceq v$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Any adjacent pair in a long word occurs in some window of length $d$, so
\eqref{eq:Lswap} permits arbitrary permutations.  Move a chosen letter to the
first position of such a window and apply \eqref{eq:Ldup}; this adds one
occurrence.  For two words with the same support, raise each multiplicity to
the coordinatewise common upper bound and then permute, proving (i).

For (ii), add occurrences and permute to derive $u\approx vt$, where $t$
may be empty.  If $t$ is nonempty, split $v$ into $d$ nonempty blocks and
substitute $t$ for $y$ in \eqref{eq:Ldrop}; this gives $vt\preceq v$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:csp}
Let $w$ be long, let $W=c(w)$, and suppose that every word in $Q$ is short
and uses only variables in $W$.  Then
\[
 \mathcal P(S)\models w\preceq Q
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 H_Q\nrightarrow\mathbf N(S).
\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
If a homomorphism $H_Q\to\mathbf N(S)$ exists, assign its nonzero singleton
values to the variables.  Every right-hand word is nonzero, whereas the
left-hand word is zero, so absorption fails.
 
Conversely, assume that there is no homomorphism but that an assignment of
subsets violates the absorption identity.  The left side must be nonempty
and equal to $\{0\}$, so all left variables are nonempty and no right word
contains zero in its value.  Every variable occurring on the right therefore
has a value not containing $0$.  Choose one element from each such value
appearing on the right, and assign arbitrary nonzero elements to isolated
variables.  The chosen elements define a homomorphism
$H_Q\to\mathbf N(S)$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $O_1,\ldots,O_t$ be a finite obstruction family for $\mathbf N(S)$.  Remove
isolated vertices from the obstructions; this does not change completeness
because $\mathbf N(S)$ is nonempty.  Every remaining obstruction contains a
relation tuple.  Let $Q_{O_i}$ be the sum of its tuple words, and let $u_i$
be any long word whose support is exactly $V(O_i)$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:csp}
gives the valid identities
\begin{equation}\label{eq:obstacle-identity}
 u_i\preceq Q_{O_i}.
\end{equation}
We claim that $L_d\cup\Psi_S$ together with these finitely many identities
is a basis.

Let $w\preceq Q$ be valid.  First apply Lemma~\ref{lem:empty} to restrict
the right-hand support.  A short left word is handled by $\Psi_S$.  If a
long right-hand word $q$ occurs, Lemma~\ref{lem:normal}(ii) gives
$w\preceq q\preceq Q$.  We are left with a long left word and only short
right-hand words.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:csp}, $H_Q\nrightarrow\mathbf N(S)$, so
some $O_i$ maps to $H_Q$.  Substitute the corresponding variables in
\eqref{eq:obstacle-identity}.  Its right side consists of words from $Q$,
while its left side is long and has support contained in $c(w)$.  Another
application of Lemma~\ref{lem:normal}(ii) absorbs $w$ into that left word
and then into $Q$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:bounded}
A nonempty finite relational structure $D$ has finite duality if and only if
$b(D)<\infty$.  If finite duality fails, then for every $M$ there is a finite
structure $H\nrightarrow D$ all of whose induced substructures on at most
$M$ vertices map to $D$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
If each member of the obstruction family has at most $M$ vertices, map an obstruction into
$H$ and take the induced substructure on its image.  It has at most $M$
vertices and cannot map to $D$, since otherwise the obstruction would map to
$D$.  Conversely, for a fixed finite signature there are only finitely many
isomorphism types on at most $M$ vertices.  Taking all types that do not map
to $D$ gives a finite obstruction family.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:localnil}
Before $\infty$ first appears in a closure derivation from $F$, every
short word $f$ already present has the following property: for every
$C\supseteq c(f)$ and every homomorphism
$\theta:H[C]\to\mathbf N(S)$, evaluation of the letters of $f$ under $\theta$
is nonzero in $S$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The map $\theta$ extends to a semigroup homomorphism
\[
 h_\theta:U_r(C)\to S,\qquad h_\theta(\infty)=0,
\]
because $S^{r+1}=\{0\}$.  Tuple words in $F$ have nonzero images.
Suppose a closure step adds a short word $f$.  Choose a factor selection
in a realization of $uw(A)v$ that produces $f$.  For each variable retain
the set of all short factors selected at its occurrences, and assign the
variables outside the left support the empty set.  All remaining letters
lie in $c(f)\subseteq C$.  The new premise is a subset of the old premise,
contains no $\infty$, and consists of words whose supports lie in $C$.
The induction hypothesis says that every such premise word has nonzero
$h_\theta$-image.  Validity of the target absorption identity, including
the chosen contexts, then forces $h_\theta(f)\ne0$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:nooverflow}
Under the preceding hypotheses, $\infty\notin c_k(F)$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Assume that a first closure step adds $\infty$, and let $Z$ be the set
before that step.  The left variables have nonempty values.  Set variables
outside the left support to the empty set.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:empty}, the
right side still has a word; hence an actual context equal to $\infty$ would
already put $\infty$ in the premise, which is impossible.
 
For each left variable choose one factor: retain $\infty$ if it occurs, and
otherwise choose a short factor of maximum length.  The resulting
singleton choices still make the left side equal to $\infty$: an existing
absorbing factor is retained, and otherwise the total length does not
decrease.  Every premise output is still a short word in $Z$.  The union
$C$ of the selected finite letters and the context letters has size at most
$r(k+2)$.  Choose a homomorphism $\theta:H[C]\to\mathbf N(S)$.  By
Lemma~\ref{lem:localnil}, all premise outputs have nonzero image, whereas
the left side, which is $\infty$, maps to zero.  This contradicts validity
of the absorption identity with its contexts.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
If finite duality fails, Lemma~\ref{lem:bounded} supplies such an $H$ for
every $k$.  Let $Q_H$ be the sum of the tuple words and let $w_H$ be a word
containing every vertex exactly once.  Since $|V|>M\ge d$, Lemma~\ref{lem:csp}
gives the valid identity $w_H\preceq Q_H$.
 
In the closure quotient $B_k$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:closure}, assign
$x_v$ the closed singleton $c_k(\{v\})$.  The left side of this identity is
$c_k(\{\infty\})$, while the right side is $c_k(F)$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:nooverflow}
shows that the identity fails in $B_k$; Lemma~\ref{lem:closure} shows that
$B_k$ satisfies all target identities involving at most $k$ variables.
Thus a finite basis, with $k$ at least its maximum number of variables,
cannot exist.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:quant}
Let $S\ne\{0\}$ be finite nilpotent of index $d$, and put $r=d-1$.
If the identity theory of $\mathcal P(S)$ is generated, possibly by an infinite
set, by identities involving at most $k$ variables, then
\[
 b(\mathbf N(S))\le r(k+2).
\]
Conversely, if $b=b(\mathbf N(S))<\infty$, then $\mathcal P(S)$ has a finite relative
basis using at most $\max\{d+1,b\}$ variables.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
If the first bound failed, there would be an $H\nrightarrow\mathbf N(S)$ all of
whose induced substructures on at most $r(k+2)$ vertices map to $\mathbf N(S)$.
The closure construction in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:nil} uses only
this one $H$ and produces an ai-semiring satisfying all valid identities on
at most $k$ variables but failing another valid identity, contradicting the
generation hypothesis.
 
Conversely, take all non-mapping structures on at most $b$ vertices as a
finite obstruction family.  The long-word identities $L_d$ use at most
$d+1$ variables, $\Psi_S$ uses at most $r$, and each obstruction identity
uses at most $b$ variables.  Repetitions of existing variables make the left
word long, so no new variables are needed.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:maxpower}
Let $S\ne\{0\}$ be finite nilpotent of index $d$.  If some
$a^{d-1}\ne0$, then $\mathcal P(S)$ is finitely based, without a commutativity
assumption.  In fact $L_d\cup\Psi_S$ is a finite relative basis.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The condition $a^{d-1}\ne0$ implies $a^j\ne0$ for every $1\le j<d$.
Consider a valid absorption identity with a long left word.  After
Lemma~\ref{lem:empty}, assign every left variable the singleton $\{a\}$.
The left side is zero and every short right word is nonzero, so the right
side must contain a long word.  Lemma~\ref{lem:normal}(ii) then proves the
identity.  Short left words are handled by $\Psi_S$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Sufficiency follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:maxpower}.  For necessity,
put $r=d-1$ and suppose that every $s^r=0$ but $S^r\ne\{0\}$.
The assumptions imply $r\ge2$.  Choose
$(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\in R_r$.  Let $L$ be the one-vertex structure with
$R_r(L)=\{(v,\ldots,v)\}$ and all other relations empty.  Then
$L\nrightarrow\mathbf N(S)$.
 
If $\mathbf N(S)$ had finite duality, the tree obstruction theorem would give a
relational tree $O$ with $O\to L$ but $O\nrightarrow\mathbf N(S)$.  Since all
relations other than $R_r$ are empty in $L$, $O$ can contain only
$R_r$-tuples.  Every such tree nevertheless maps to $\mathbf N(S)$.  Assign
the vertices of a root tuple successively to $a_1,\ldots,a_r$.  When a new
tuple is attached, exactly one vertex has already been assigned, say the
value $a_i$.  Put $a_i$ in the shared coordinate and place the remaining
$r-1$ factors, in any order, on the new vertices.  Commutativity makes the
product of every tuple equal to the nonzero product $a_1\cdots a_r$.
A tree with no tuple maps to any nonzero element.  This contradiction shows that
$\mathbf N(S)$ has no finite duality, and Theorem~\ref{thm:nil} gives
nonfinite basis.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:permuted}
Let $S$ be finite nilpotent of index $d=r+1$, suppose that $s^r=0$ for
every $s\in S$, and assume that some $a_1,\ldots,a_r$ have nonzero product
in every permutation.  Then $\mathcal P(S)$ is nonfinitely based.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The tree extension above needs only nonzeroness of every permutation, not
equality of the resulting products.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:directed}
Let $L=\{a,b,c,0\}$, with the only nonzero binary product $ab=c$.
All products of length three are zero, so associativity holds and every
element has square zero.  The only nontrivial relation of $\mathbf N(L)$ is the
directed edge $a\to b$; $c$ is isolated.  A finite directed graph maps to
this structure exactly when it contains no directed walk of length two.
Necessity is immediate.  For sufficiency, assign $a$ to vertices with an
outgoing edge, $b$ to vertices with an incoming edge, and any value to the
remaining vertices.  The absence of a length-two directed walk prevents a
vertex from receiving both prescriptions.  A directed path of length two is
therefore a finite obstruction, and Theorem~\ref{thm:nil} gives a finite
basis for $\mathcal P(L)$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:nonhereditary}
Let $T=\{a,b,c,0\}$ with $ab=ba=c$ as the only nonzero products.  It is
commutative of index three and every square is zero, so $\mathcal P(T)$ is
nonfinitely based.  Now let
\[
 S=\{a,b,c,u,v,0\},\qquad ab=ba=c,\quad u^2=v,
\]
with all other binary products zero.  All products of length three are zero,
so $S$ is associative, while $u^2\ne0$.  Proposition~\ref{prop:maxpower}
therefore gives a finite basis for $\mathcal P(S)$.  Nevertheless $T$ is a
subsemigroup of $S$, and $\{u,v,0\}$ is an ideal whose Rees quotient is
isomorphic to $T$.  The inclusion and quotient map induce, respectively, an
embedding and a surjective homomorphism of full power semirings.  Thus the
finite basis property is not preserved by these subsemirings or homomorphic
images.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:logical}
Let $S\ne\{0\}$ be finite nilpotent of index $d$, put $D=\mathbf N(S)$,
and let $C$ be a core of $D$. The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),nosep]
\item $\mathcal P(S)$ is finitely based;
\item $D$ has finite duality;
\item $\operatorname{CSP}(D)$ is first-order definable;
\item $D$ has a finite complete obstruction family consisting of relational
trees;
\item $C^2$ dismantles to $\Delta_C$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:nil} gives (i)$\Leftrightarrow$(ii). The equivalence of
(ii), (iii), and (iv) is \cite[Theorem~2.5]{LLT}; the first-order
characterization originates in the work of Atserias \cite{Ats}.
The equivalence with (v) follows from \cite[Theorem~5.7]{LLT} and the
core case established immediately before that theorem. Indeed, $D$ and
$C$ admit homomorphisms to each other, so they define the same
homomorphism class of finite structures.

For completeness, the sentence in (iii) can be written directly from
any obstruction family $O_1,\ldots,O_t$ in (ii). Delete isolated vertices
from these obstructions. For a remaining obstruction $O$, put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:canonical-query}
 \chi_O=
 \exists(x_v)_{v\in V(O)}\,
 \bigwedge_{j=1}^{d-1}\ \bigwedge_{(v_1,\ldots,v_j)\in R_j(O)}
 R_j(x_{v_1},\ldots,x_{v_j}).
\end{equation}
No distinctness conditions are imposed on the variables. Consequently
$H\models\chi_O$ if and only if $O\to H$. The sentence
$\bigwedge_{i=1}^t\neg\chi_{O_i}$ therefore defines
$\operatorname{CSP}(D)$; for an empty obstruction family it is the
identically true sentence.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
Fix $h\in G$.  A prescribed-phase instance $H$ consists of a finite vertex
set $V$, a phase map $\nu:V\to\mathbb F_2$, and finitely many ordered tuples of
lengths $1,\ldots,D-1$.  A satisfying assignment
$\theta:V\to S$ must obey $\rho(\theta(v))=\nu(v)$ and must make the product
of every listed tuple different from $h$.  Repeated coordinates are allowed.
The induced subinstance on a vertex set retains the prescribed phases and all
tuples contained in that set.  The empty induced instance is declared
satisfiable.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:phase}
Suppose that for some $h\in G$ and every $M\ge1$ there is an unsatisfiable
prescribed-phase instance $H$ whose induced subinstances on at most $M$
vertices are all satisfiable.  Then $\mathcal P(S)$ is nonfinitely based and its
identity theory has no basis with a bounded number of variables.
More precisely, for $k\ge1$, if
one unsatisfiable instance has every induced subinstance on at most
$2(D-1)(k+2)$ vertices satisfiable, then the identities of $\mathcal P(S)$ on at
most $k$ variables do not generate its full identity theory.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:guards}
If $H$ is unsatisfiable, the corresponding identity
\eqref{eq:guard0} or \eqref{eq:guard1} is valid in $\mathcal P(S)$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
If one variable is empty, the left side is empty.  Suppose all values are
nonempty.  If the projection of $z$ is the whole group, its displayed power
term covers the left side.  If the projection of some $x_v$ is the whole
group, the displayed long term covering that variable does so.  Since the
left side is long and lies in $G$, it remains to consider singleton
projections.
 
For \eqref{eq:guard0}, the left side is $e$.  If $z$ has phase zero, $z^t$
supplies $e$.  If $z$ has phase one and a vertex has a phase different from
its prescribed phase, the term $z^tx_v$ or $x_v^t$ supplies $e$.  In the
remaining case all vertex phases are prescribed correctly.  Selecting one
element from each variable value gives a forbidden tuple by unsatisfiability,
so $e\in Q_H$.
 
For \eqref{eq:guard1}, if $z$ has phase zero then both the left side and
$z^{2t}$ are $e$.  If $z$ has phase one, the left side is $g$, and every
phase error is covered by the displayed long term for that vertex.  With all
phases correct, unsatisfiability again gives $g\in Q_H$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:phase-exclusion}
The forbidden group element $\eta$ does not belong to $c_k(F^+)$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Suppose a first closure step adds $\eta$.  The left and right contexts can
be represented by two additional variables, so the step comes from a valid
absorption identity on at most $\ell=k+2$ variables.  Set variables outside
the left support to the empty set.  For each nonempty left-variable value,
retain the longest short factor of phase zero, the longest short factor of
phase one (when present), and every group element originally in that value.

Every factor selection producing $\eta$ can be replaced by representatives of
the same phase of no smaller length, while group factors are kept.  Thus the
left side still produces $\eta$.  The union $C$ of the retained letters has
at most $2r(k+2)$ vertices.  Choose a satisfying assignment on $H[C]$.
The invariant maps every reduced short premise away from $h$, and the only
group premise is $\bar\eta$.  The left side maps to $h$, contradicting
validity of the target absorption identity.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
In the closure quotient, assign $z$ the closed singleton $c_k(\{\gamma\})$
and $x_v$ the closed singleton $c_k(\{v\})$.  The left side of the
appropriate guard identity is $c_k(\{\eta\})$.  Every displayed long
right-hand term evaluates to $\bar\eta$, so the right side is
$c_k(F^+)$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:phase-exclusion} says that this valid identity
fails in the quotient, while Lemma~\ref{lem:closure} says that all target
identities on at most $k$ variables hold there.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:fibre}
Let $T=\rho^{-1}(e)$.  If $\mathcal P(S)$ is finitely based, then $\mathcal P(T)$ is
finitely based.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The element $e$ is a zero of $T$, and $T^D=\{e\}$.  If $T=\{e\}$ there is
nothing to prove.  Otherwise let $d\le D$ be the nilpotency index of $T$.
If $\mathcal P(T)$ were nonfinitely based, Theorem~\ref{thm:nil} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:bounded} would give arbitrarily large locally satisfiable
instances for $\mathbf N(T)$.  Give all vertices phase zero, keep the
constraints of lengths below $d$, omit the others, and forbid $e$.
Any vertex occurring in a constraint must take a value different from $e$.
Values at isolated vertices may be replaced by any element of
$T\setminus\{e\}$.  Hence satisfiability is equivalent to the existence of
a homomorphism to $\mathbf N(T)$.  These are instances of
Theorem~\ref{thm:phase}, contradicting finite basis of
$\mathcal P(S)$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:affine}
Let $w$ be a nonempty word with support $W$, let
$Q=q_1+\cdots+q_s$ be nonempty with $c(q_j)\subseteq W$, and let
$\alpha,\beta_j\in\mathbb F_2^W$ be the parity vectors of $w,q_j$, respectively.
Then
\[
 \mathcal P(C_2)\models w\preceq Q
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \bigcup_j c(q_j)=W,\qquad
 \alpha\in\operatorname{aff}\{\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_s\}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
If a left variable is absent on the right, assign it the whole group and
all other variables the identity singleton; absorption fails.  For singleton
assignments $b\in\mathbb F_2^W$, validity says that some
$(\beta_j+\alpha)\cdot b=0$.  If $\alpha$ is outside the affine hull, put
$a=\beta_1+\alpha$ and
$L=\operatorname{span}\{\beta_j+\beta_1\}$.  A linear functional vanishing
on $L$ and taking value one on $a$ supplies a $b$ for which all these
dot products are one, a contradiction.
 
Conversely, an empty left-variable value makes the left side empty.
Assume that all values are nonempty.  If a variable value is the whole group, support coverage makes
some right word evaluate to the whole group.  Otherwise all values are
singletons.  The affine condition is equivalent to
$\alpha=\sum_{j\in J}\beta_j$ for a nonempty set $J$ of odd cardinality.
Over $\mathbb F_2$, an odd sum of bits equals one of the summands, so the left
value equals a right value.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:c2basis}
Relative to the ai-semiring identities, $\mathcal P(C_2)$ has the finite basis
\[
 xy\approx yx,\qquad x^3\approx x.
\]
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
The four group subsets satisfy these identities.  Commutativity and
$x^3\approx x$ reduce each positive multiplicity to one or two according
to its parity, so words with the same support and parity are provably equal.
For a valid absorption identity, first
delete outside variables and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:affine} to obtain an odd
index set $J$.  Put
\[
 v=\left(\prod_{j\in J}q_j\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^s q_j^2\right).
\]
The words $v$ and $w$ have the same support and parity, so the two displayed
identities prove $v\approx w$.  Moreover
$v\preceq Q^{|J|+2s}\approx Q$ by distributivity and reduction of odd powers.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:lift}
Let $S$ have an ideal $G\cong C_2$ with $S^d\subseteq G$, $d\ge2$.  Suppose
there are elements $a_0,a_1\in S$ of phases zero and one such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lift}
 \{a_0,a_1\}^{\,j}\cap G=\varnothing\qquad(1\le j<d).
\end{equation}
Then $\mathcal P(S)$ is finitely based.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Let $E_d$ consist of all adjacent transposition identities in a length-$d$
window and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ed}
 x_1\cdots x_d\approx x_1^3x_2\cdots x_d .
\end{equation}
Long-word values depend only on group projections, and
$\mathcal P(C_2)\models x^3\approx x$, so $E_d$ is valid.  The window argument
from Lemma~\ref{lem:normal} allows arbitrary permutations and adds two
occurrences of any chosen variable.  Hence two long words with the same
support and parity vector can be made equal by $E_d$.
 
Add
\begin{equation}\label{eq:triple}
 U_dV_dW_d\preceq U_d+V_d+W_d,
\end{equation}
where $U_d,V_d,W_d$ are length-$d$ words on pairwise disjoint variable
sets.  This is valid because the product of any three elements of $C_2$ is
one of them; if a set value is empty, the left side is empty.  Splitting
each of three long words into $d$ nonempty blocks gives the corresponding
instance of \eqref{eq:triple}.  Consequently, if $R$ is any nonempty sum
of long words, distributivity yields $R^3\preceq R$.  Multiplicative
monotonicity and induction give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:oddR}
 R^{2m+1}\preceq R\qquad(m\ge0).
\end{equation}
 
On $r=d-1$ variables take a finite word library containing all short words
and one long representative for each nonempty support and parity vector.
Let $\mathcal W'_r$ denote this library and set
\[
 \Psi'_S=\left\{u\preceq\sum_{q\in Q}q:
 u\in\mathcal W'_r,\ \varnothing\ne Q\subseteq\mathcal W'_r,\
 \mathcal P(S)\models u\preceq\sum_{q\in Q}q\right\}.
\]
If a valid absorption identity has a short left word, empty-set elimination
restricts its right side to at most $r$ variables.  Long-word normalization
then reduces it to a member of $\Psi'_S$ after renaming variables.
 
Now let $w$ be long.  Restrict the right support and split the right side
into its long part $Q_L$ and short part.  For arbitrary group-subset values
$B_i$, lift them to $A_i=\{a_b:b\in B_i\}$.  Condition \eqref{eq:lift}
keeps every short right word outside $G$, while long words are evaluated by
their phase projections.  Nonempty singleton phase assignments show that
$Q_L$ is nonempty, and the same lifting for arbitrary phase subsets gives
$\mathcal P(C_2)\models w\preceq Q_L$.  Write $Q_L=q_1+\cdots+q_s$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:affine}, choose an odd
index set $J$ and form
\[
 v=\left(\prod_{j\in J}q_j\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^s q_j^2\right).
\]
The words $v$ and $w$ have the same support and parity, so $E_d\vdash
w\approx v$, while \eqref{eq:oddR} gives
$v\preceq Q_L^{|J|+2s}\preceq Q_L$.  Thus
\[
 E_d\cup\{\eqref{eq:triple}\}\cup\Psi'_S
\]
is a finite relative basis.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The ideal of $N\times C_2$ is $\{0\}\times C_2$, and its identity fibre is
$N\times\{e\}\cong N$.  The necessary implication follows from
Corollary~\ref{cor:fibre}, without commutativity.  If $a^{d-1}\ne0$, take
$a_0=(a,e)$ and $a_1=(a,g)$.  Every product of fewer than $d$ such elements
has first coordinate $a^j\ne0$, so \eqref{eq:lift} holds and
Theorem~\ref{thm:lift} gives finite basis.  For commutative $N$,
Corollary~\ref{cor:comm} says that this is exactly the condition for
$\mathcal P(N)$ to be finitely based.  If $N$ is the one-point zero semigroup,
the product is $C_2$ and Corollary~\ref{cor:c2basis} applies.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The coordinate projection
\[
 \mathcal P(N\times C_2)\longrightarrow\mathcal P(N)\times\mathcal P(C_2)
\]
loses the pairing information inside a subset and is generally not an
isomorphism.  The proof above works with arbitrary subset assignments and
does not make this identification.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:five}
Let $S_5=\{e,g,a,b,c\}$, with
$\rho(e)=\rho(c)=e$ and $\rho(g)=\rho(a)=\rho(b)=g$.  Apart from
$ab=ba=c$, let every binary product be the product of the two group phases.
Then $S_5$ is commutative, $S_5^3=C_2$,
$\mathcal P(\rho^{-1}(e))$ is finitely based, and $\mathcal P(S_5)$ is nonfinitely based.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
The multiplication is displayed in Table~\ref{tab:five}.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\caption{Multiplication in $S_5$.}\label{tab:five}
\centering
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{12pt}
\begin{tabular}{cccccc}
\toprule
$\cdot$&$e$&$g$&$a$&$b$&$c$\\
\midrule
$e$&$e$&$g$&$g$&$g$&$e$\\
$g$&$g$&$e$&$e$&$e$&$g$\\
$a$&$g$&$e$&$e$&$c$&$g$\\
$b$&$g$&$e$&$c$&$e$&$g$\\
$c$&$e$&$g$&$g$&$g$&$e$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Every binary product is either in the group or is $c$; multiplying once
more always enters the group and gives the product of the three phases.
Thus all bracketings of a triple agree, and the table is associative.
The group is contained in $S_5^3$, so $S_5^3=C_2$.
 
The identity fibre $\{e,c\}$ has all binary products equal to $e$, so its
full power semiring is finitely based by Proposition~\ref{prop:maxpower}.
In the odd fibre $\{g,a,b\}$, a binary product is different from $e$ exactly
for the ordered pairs $(a,b)$ and $(b,a)$.
 
For every $M$, take an odd cycle of length greater than $M$, prescribe phase
one at all vertices, and forbid $e$ on every oriented edge.  A satisfying
assignment would have to alternate $a$ and $b$ around the cycle, which is
impossible.  Every induced subgraph on at most $M$ vertices is a disjoint
union of paths and isolated vertices and can be alternately assigned $a,b$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:phase} therefore gives nonfinite basis.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
